Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson said that despite Apple's claims of reviewing submitted content, blatant App Store rating manipulation has gone undetected.

He said that although he doesn't actively seek out fraud on the App Store, he stumbles across it fairly often, and mentioned the latest example...

The App Store is a 'safe and trusted place'

Apple has consistently taken a hard stance against any antitrust measures that would involve third-party app stores or iPhone sideloading, only relenting when legally compelled to do so. Even so, it continues to defend itself relentlessly.

The company claims it does so not for the money, but to protect iPhone users from malicious software. For instance, Apple said last year that it blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, many developers have reservations about the 'App Store is a safe place' narrative, and have pointed to numerous scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers who had all their Bitcoin stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store rating manipulation

App Store rating manipulation has been a longstanding problem, with companies in mainland China even renting out 'iPhone farms' to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for his StopTheMadness Safari extension) pointed out the latest example of what he described as 'widespread and obvious' review fraud on the App Store. The app in question is TabControl Extension.

He said when he stumbled upon the app, it was the number 12 paid Safari extension on the US Mac App Store, and featured a screenshot that was clearly an AI-generated fake.

Another thing to note is that the fake screenshot reads '4.9 stars (out of 5)', giving the impression that this is the App Store user rating for the app... Using App Store screenshots to make false claims is a common scam tactic I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself, but also the App Store listing and metadata, including screenshots. The claims in scam app screenshots are often absurdly obvious at a glance, yet Apple approves them anyway... Apple claims the App Store protects users from dishonest developers. If App Store review can't even catch this, what exactly is it doing? In fact, App Store review wouldn't even need to dig as deep as I did. The '4.9 stars (out of 5)' in the screenshot itself is already a red flag. Apple has all the rating and review records for every country, and they know full well this is false advertising. I don't even need to download the damn app to know the developer is trying to scam people.

As he pointed out, if a developer is willing to scam you out of money to sell apps in the first place, you certainly don't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, catching all App Store fraud is an impossible task, but fake reviews are absurdly common, and instances like this should be blatantly obvious to Apple. It's hard to understand how this extension ever got approved.

At the very least, Apple should establish a mechanism that automatically triggers a fresh, stricter review of any app that breaks into any top-chart ranking, examining both the app itself and the claims it makes.
